1849 Establishment of the company On February 9, 1849, Heintze & Freudenberg was established as a tannery with 50 employees in Müllheimer Tal, a valley near Weinheim in southern Germany. From the very beginning, the company was intensively involved in international trade, including exports to the USA, the United Kingdom and France. 1850 First innovation Following the introduction of patent leather in 1850, the company flourished. By 1855, patent leather accounted for more than 80 % of production. 1874 Establishment of Carl Freudenberg In 1874, partner Leopold Heintze died and Carl Johann Freudenberg became sole proprietor. Trading as Carl Freudenberg, the company became Germany's largest tannery. 1887 First business principles In 1887, at a time when the company already employed more than 500 associates, a new generation joined the management, with Friedrich Carl and Hermann Ernst Freudenberg, the sons of the founder, both becoming partners. On this occasion, Carl Johann Freudenberg wrote down his business principles for his sons. To this day, they form the basis of Freudenberg's Guiding Principles. 1904 Chrome tanning Between 1900 and 1904, in the course of his own experiments, Hermann Ernst Freudenberg developed a chrome tanning process of the type already used in the USA. This process was based on the use of chrome salts or chrome liquor instead of the tanning liquor previously used, which consisted of a variety of vegetable materials (mainly oak bark). This invention reduced production time from several months to a few weeks. The leather was waterproof, easy to care for and had a homogeneous surface texture. Freudenberg was one of the first companies in Europe capable of producing high-quality chrome-tanned calf leather. With the introduction of chrome tanning, Freudenberg became the largest leather manufacturer in Europe. 1914-18 First World War Following the outbreak of the First World War, the leather business slumped dramatically. Due to the mandatory military draft, the number of associates dropped drastically, too – from more than 2,500 to 800. Women took over the work of their husbands who had been drafted but, after their return, the men reclaimed their jobs again. 1921 First business relations with India and China The company started business relations with India for raw material purchasing. The first business relations with China were also developed around this time (1923). 1929 The first seals The Great Depression brought the entire German leather industry to the brink of ruin. The sales price for a tanned calf hide fell far below the purchase price of a raw hide. To ensure the survival of the company in these troubled economic times, managing directors Hans, Otto, Richard and Walter Freudenberg looked for ways to diversify the company’s operations and to develop entirely new products. In 1929, the company introduced a leather seal for the growing automobile industry of a type already produced in North America. 1932 Development of the Simmerring Freudenberg’s revolutionary new Simmerring ushered the company into a new era in Sealing Technology. The Simmerring – named after its inventor, Walther Simmer – was a radial shaft seal which replaced the felt seals that had been used to date. The original Simmerring consisted of a steel sheet housing with a rubber sleeve installed inside. The radial force and the sealing performance of the Simmerring were also improved by using a garter spring. 1933 The shoe business Freudenberg took over the shoe manufacturing and sales business of Conrad Tack in Burg, close to Magdeburg. Tack had faced troubled times in the wake of the Great Depression and had huge debts to Freudenberg as a result of unpaid invoices for leather supplies. Negotiations concerning a takeover had already begun in the fall of 1932. When the situation for the Jewish proprietors, the Krojanker family, became untenable from 1933 onwards, Freudenberg purchased the shares owned by the family at market price. The company operated a network of more than 140 independent retail outlets. Freudenberg took advantage of this situation to employ associates opposed to National Socialism, including people who were actively involved in the resistance efforts of former Hessian Minister of the Interior, Wilhelm Leuschner. In this way, they were safe from persecution by the regime. Freudenberg employed more than 3,500 associates. 1936 Simmerring with rubber seal lip Freudenberg replaced leather with rubber as a seal material. In 1936, the company developed a seal ring made from Perbunan. This material features high temperature and swelling resistance when exposed to engine lubricating oil. The Simmerring made from Perbunan represented a quantum leap in sealing technology. As a result, the Simmerring was the first seal to ensure optimum sealing of rotating shafts such as automobile drive shafts. The innovation made Freudenberg the market leader in sealing technology. 1938 Start of nonwoven production In 1938, Freudenberg started production of the newly developed Viledon synthetic leather, which was used as a leather replacement material for bags and suitcases. The backing material was a nonwoven that Freudenberg had been developing since 1936. The originator of Freudenberg's first nonwoven product was Carl Ludwig Nottebohm. Perbunan synthetic rubber was also used for Nora shoe soles, with production starting in 1938. 1948 Vileda Production of Vlieseline interlinings and Vileda cloths, both nonwoven products, started. These two new products gave rise to entirely new business areas. Freudenberg forged ahead with diversification. 1950 First manufacturing company abroad Freudenberg founded its first production company outside Germany in 1950 in the United States. Interlinings for the clothing industry were produced at a plant in Lowell, Massachusetts. Another product area was opened up when nora® rubber floor coverings were launched. 1957 Filter systems and vibration control The next steps in diversification followed in 1957. In addition to the sealing technology business, the company started activities in vibration control technology. Shock absorbers, vibration dampers of various types and ultra bushings were produced under the Metalastik (later Vibracoustic) brand. In the same year, the first filters were produced, laying the foundation for the technical nonwovens product range. 1960 Partners in Japan 1960 saw the start of two key partnerships. In the field of sealing technology a close business partnership was established with Nippon Oil Seal Industry Company (NOK) in Tokyo. In the nonwovens sector, Freudenberg Vliesstoffe and its Japanese partners founded the Japan Vilene Company, also headquartered in Tokyo. Freudenberg employed more than 11,000 associates worldwide. 1966 Klüber Lubrication acquired In 1966, Freudenberg acquired lubricant manufacturer Klüber Lubrication in Munich. The fact that Theodor Klüber sold his company to Freudenberg has its roots in the pacifist beliefs of Richard Freudenberg. In 1967, Freudenberg launched the knobbed floor-covering Norament, later to become a classic product. The first major project for the new product was Frankfurt airport. 1970 Spunbonded nonwovens An innovation by Dr. Ludwig Hartmann leads to a new manufacturing technology for spunbonded nonwovens. The first spunbonded nonwoven plant started production in Kaiserslautern in 1970. 1977 Entry into the electronics sector To spread business risk and access new markets, Freudenberg started producing electromechanical components and printed circuitry in 1977. From the 1980s onwards, alongside Japanese partner NOK, the Group developed the market for flexible printed circuit boards for use in electrical and electronic equipment and components. 1983 Internationalisation of the corporate logo As Freudenberg became increasingly international, the "W" for Weinheim in the logo no longer reflected the nature of the Group. For this reason, the Freudenberg name was incorporated into an integrated logo in 1983. The wave at the bottom edge of the logo reflects the sine curve shown on the instruments used for ensuring the quality of Freudenberg technical products. 1984 Freudenberg Foundation The Freudenberg Stiftung, a non-profit foundation, was established in 1984. Members of the Freudenberg family transferred shares and other deposits to the foundation. The Foundation is a Partner in Freudenberg, albeit without voting rights. In accordance with the statutes of the Foundation, income from its participation in Freudenberg is used for promoting science and education as well as for reinforcing peaceful coexistence within society. The main focus of the Foundation's activities is on children and young people. 1985 Expansion of household product range 1985 saw the launch of the vileda wet mop, one of the most successful products ever developed by vileda. For the first time, vileda offered a complete floor wiping system consisting of a mop with bucket and wringer. 1989 First cabin air filters for cars The first cabin air filters for cars were launched under the micronAir® brand. Today, Freudenberg is the world market leader for cabin air filters. The North American activities of Freudenberg and its Japanese partner NOK were combined in a joint venture, Freudenberg-NOK General Partnership. 1995 First production in China Freudenberg opened its first production facilities in China. These were seals factories in Changchun and Wuxi, established in cooperation with its Japanese partner NOK, and an interlinings production plant in Suzhou, where the cooperation partner was Japan Vilene Company. 1996 FOKUS In a major project entitled FOCUS (Freudenberg Organisation for Customer-Responsive Corporate Structure), Freudenberg adapted its structure to reflect the company’s broad and international orientation. Freudenberg was subsequently divided into Business Groups, capable of operating independently in line with constantly changing market requirements. Freudenberg became a Group with decentralised management structures. The new, more flexible Business Groups could now focus even better on their respective markets and core competencies. At the same time, they had the freedom to streamline their product ranges and optimise their sales channels. 1997 First mechatronic seal components Thanks to the development of encoder technology, the Simmerring was able to assume additional functions beyond those of a simple seal. The encoder forms an integrated sensor system that can be used, for example, to measure rotation speed and control an ABS or engine management system. 1999 Microfibre nonwovens With Evolon technology, Freudenberg developed an entirely new spunbonded microfilament nonwoven production process which set new standards. The Group employed about 30,000 associates worldwide. 2001 Freudenberg enters fuel cell technology Freudenberg Fuel Cell Components Technology was founded in 2001. The company pools the expertise of various Freudenberg companies and develops components for the highly promising fuel cell sector. In 2001, Freudenberg sold the last part of its shoe business, Elefanten GmbH (a manufacturer of children's shoes). The Tack shoe retail chain had already been sold in 1999. In 2002, the Management Board decided to discontinue Freudenberg’s original leather business due to increasingly unfavourable market conditions. Major customers were moving into other business areas, restructuring their organisations and discontinuing their manufacturing businesses. At the same time, raw material prices were constantly increasing in the wake of animal diseases such as BSE and foot and mouth disease. 2004 Acquisition of Burgmann Dichtungswerke In 2004, Freudenberg completed the largest acquisition in its history. By taking over Burgmann Dichtungswerke in Wolfratshausen near Munich, Freudenberg added mechanical seals to its seals business. Activities in the oil and gas industry were intensified, leading ultimately to a partnership with the Japanese Eagle Industries and the foundation of the internationally active EagleBurgmann Group. In addition, Freudenberg acquired Chem-Trend, a specialist release agent producer to expand the Group’s Chemical Specialties business. With the acquisition of the North American Jenline Industries, a manufacturer of rubber products, Freudenberg entered the medical technology sector. 2006 Expansion into new markets Freudenberg made further acquisitions to increase its activities in the oil and gas industry and medical technology. In 2006, the oil and gas business was strengthened by the acquisition of Imperial Rubber and Urethane Corporation in Nisku/Canada. In 2006, the Group also acquired Helix Medical, a manufacturer of high-quality precision-moulded parts, as well as tubes for the medical technology, pharma and biotech markets. Freudenberg opened its first plant in Russia in Nizhny Novogorod, where Freudenberg Politex now produces polyester nonwovens for the construction industry. With the sale of Freudenberg Bausysteme KG and its Nora® brand, Freudenberg sold its floor-covering business to a consortium of investors (capiton AG and L-EA). The company currently operates in Weinheim under the name “NORA Systems”. 2008-2009 Global financial and economic crisis The deepest economic crisis since World War II was triggered by the collapse of the financial market in North America in 2008. Within just a few weeks, the crisis spread across the world, leading to immense liquidity shortages. In addition to ongoing instabilities in the real economy, this situation had an extremely adverse effect on industrial production worldwide. Freudenberg did not escape the full impact of the crisis, especially as the automotive industry and the mechanical engineering sector – Freudenberg’s most important customers – were both severely affected. In 2009, average annual sales dropped by almost 40 percent. Despite the early implementation of countermeasures, such as rigorous cash management, stricter accounts receivable management and the streamlining of production capacities, Freudenberg reported a decline in sales of around 17 percent. In line with local laws and other legal regulations, Freudenberg implemented flexible work programmes to ensure that the company could retain as many associates as possible. The great variety of measures implemented and the improvement of workflows meant that Freudenberg was able to emerge from the crisis with renewed strength. 2010-2012 Further strategic milestones The new Business Groups Freudenberg Oil & Gas, Helix Medical and Freudenberg Schwab (rail vehicles) were established on January 1, 2011, breaking new ground in strategic growth areas. Freudenberg developed a new resource-efficient production process for metal rings that almost entirely avoids waste. The company was awarded “Der Deutsche Innovationspreis 2011” (a German prize for innovation) for the highly efficient welding and laser technology used in the Simmerring production process. Freudenberg Household Products expanded its activities in Asia. In India, Freudenberg established the joint venture Freudenberg Gala Household Products with the company’s Indian partners. In 2011, the Group acquired the operational business Trade & Investment in Asia Limited (TIA) with offices in China, Hong Kong, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia and Taiwan. In 2012, Freudenberg SE was established to pool all business operations. The objective was to make Freudenberg corporate structures simpler and more transparent. In the same year, the joint venture TrelleborgVibracoustic was established, pooling the vibration control business of the Freudenberg company Vibracoustic and Sweden’s Trelleborg AS.

His name is Carl Johann Freudenberg. The success of the technology company bearing his name can be traced back to him. It was 175 years ago – on February 9, 1849 – that he and a partner founded a leather factory in Weinheim. The company’s unique rise followed. Their enterprise would become a global company whose story has been superbly documented in a modern archive as well as other sources. But what does the record tell us about Carl Johann’s personality, about him as a human being? How are his thinking and actions continuing to shape Freudenberg’s corporate values today? The detectives at the Freudenberg Archives are on the case. Carl Johann Freudenberg with his family Carl Johann Freudenberg “Imagine the founder of a startup who has just become a father for the third time and, in the middle of a revolution, buys a small insolvent business with support from his father-in-law,” suggests Freudenberg Archivist Julia Schneider. Admittedly, this is a simplified image of Carl Johann, but it shows he had no shortage of confidence. He was fortunate to gather the right elements for a steady, step-by-step rise from apprentice to co-owner, and eventually, the sole proprietor of his own company. What were these elements? What led him, as a 30-year-old father and family man, to look ahead to success during a time of great uncertainty? “The right character traits are part of the answer. So are the right associations in his business and personal life,” Schneider says. Georg Wilhelm Freudenberg, around 1811. It all begins with an early, fateful event. Carl Johann was just nine years old when he lost his father, a man who had led a hard life. Georg Wilhelm Freudenberg ran “Zum Löwen,” an inn in Hachenburg, a town between Cologne and Frankfurt. But it was a time of severe poverty in the early industrial era. In early 1829, the inn had to be closed, and its innkeeper had to make a drastic career change. He found a job at the customs house in Weilburg an der Lahn, but unfortunately, he passed away shortly after. The date was March 9, 1829. His son Carl Johann had accompanied him from Hachenburg and was the only one with him at the time. His childhood was over. His family mourned and struggled for financial survival. His mother took him and his five siblings to Neuwied, where relatives made sure they would not starve. At 14, Carl Johann was on his own. He began an apprenticeship in his uncle’s leather shop in Mannheim, 200 kilometers (about 124 miles) away. It was a long distance to travel at the time. “The family’s hardship triggered something in Carl Johann and gave him the urge to make something of himself,” Schneider says. “We see this in his later years when he rose to become a kind of self-made man – thanks to his ambition, industriousness and thrift.” Johann Baptist Sammet Mannheim National Theatre, 1782 Carl Johann quickly found himself. He discovered his strengths. He supported himself as an apprentice to his uncle, Johann Baptist Sammet, and partner Heinrich Christian Heintze in Mannheim, which was a vibrant, large city and quite a contrast to his hometown. “At this time, he notices the positive impact of his own performance and his own capabilities on his life. This gives him the self-confidence to continue the mission of making something of himself,” Schneider says. His industriousness and ambition drove him on. The young man not only served customers from behind the trading house’s counter and made deliveries – with the help of earnings from the leather business, but he also managed to run a cigar store, improving his finances. Freudenberg, who never attended secondary school, learned French and English. Additionally, he attended the National theater Mannheim where he moved with growing confidence in respected and international circles and continued to shine in his uncle’s company. As a result, in 1844, he was permitted to invest his money into the firm and acquired 20% of its shares as a silent partner. Carl Johann Freudenberg's wife Sophie Later the same year: Carl Johann married Sophie Martenstein, whom he had met at a choral event during the spring of the previous year. Martenstein came from a wealthy family from Worms. Her father, a spice merchant, was a respected businessman. He approved the match, but he no doubt looked beyond young Freudenberg’s heart, character and personal appearance in making the decision. There were economic realities to consider, including the suitor’s net worth and his professional success. In her memoirs, Sophie wrote: “The conviction that he was gaining a good, capable son-in-law who had already saved up 5,000 guilders [the equivalent of about €100,000 today], led my father to entrust his only daughter to him.” Children came along over the next few years: The first arrivals were two daughters, Elise and Luise, although the latter died young. When son Friedrich Carl was born in 1848 in Mannheim, the Baden Revolution was already raging. The founder of the company with his wife and six of their children in this hand-coloured photograph from 1857. Company founder Carl Johann Freudenberg, around 1870. He was over 50 years old at the time. Sophie Freudenberg, wife of Carl Johann Freudenberg, around 1870. The founder's youngest son, Hermann Ernst Freudenberg, photographed in 1879. The 1811 painting shows Katharina Elisabeth Freudenberg, Carl Johann‘s mother. Friedrich Carl Freudenberg, the eldest son of the founder, around 1895, when he and his brother were already partners. This house, called Carlshof, in Weinheim was completed in 1866 for Carl Johann Freudenberg. He lived here until his death in 1898. Painting of Weinheim 1857 with the Freudenberg lacquer factory on the left, partly hidden by trees. A view of the tanners‘ quarter in Weinheim, around 1890. Although the company was never directly based here, the tanners’ quarter is the source of the long tradition of the leather production in Weinheim, which goes back to the Middle Ages. The site of the tannery in the Müllheim valley in Weinheim, around 1880. Heinrich Christian Heintze Battle at Großsachsen, near Weinheim, in June 1849 (Image source: Museum of the city of Weinheim). What was happening on Carl Johann’s doorstep in Mannheim? At stake was nothing less than press freedom, trial by jury and a German national state with a freely elected parliament. Until that point, the country was a patchwork of independent territories, including the Grand Duchy of Baden, where Mannheim was located. The revolutionaries were divided into two camps, one liberal-constitutional and the other radical-democratic. Disorder reigned in Mannheim. There were calls for radical change. Thousands attended revolutionary peoples’ assemblies, and countless more of them were held across the entire country. There were pitched battles. “Business people who generally want stable political conditions viewed the events anxiously. That was true for our founder as well,” Schneider says. He may have suspected that fate was about to put him to the test – again. The country was in the throes of political storms. In their midst, the bank that had handled the company’s bills of exchange and financed its leather business collapsed. The firm fell into difficulty and had to be dissolved in 1848. “Let’s return to the concepts of luck and the right ingredients,” Schneider says. “Freudenberg has the good fortune to be able to turn the crisis into an opportunity. He now has a strong family behind him who can give him seed money.” His father-in-law, who thought highly of him, made the capital available to his daughter Sophie so she could help her husband with a plan to acquire part of the company. At the time, it was a progressive notion to involve a daughter in business matters. Nine decades later, Friedrich Carl, who was born during the year of revolution, wrote in his memoirs: “Since the liquidation required the departure of the two owners, my father was able to choose between them. He chose Mr. Heintze. The firm of Heintze & Freudenberg ended up in Weinheim, taking over the small calf leather tannery in 1849.” Why did he buy into a leather factory with Heintze and not into the leather shop with his uncle? For an entrepreneur, the leather factory had broader opportunities for designs and growth than “just” a leather shop. “This shows Carl Johann’s entrepreneurial vision,” says Schneider. And there was something else: “The conviction that he could pull this off in turbulent times is because he had already extricated himself from a financial crisis as a young man. His personal qualities had made him a success. In a sense, it was a repetition of something that he had already handled. This time, he was determined to use his experience and strengths to his advantage.” Thus, in the middle of a revolution, he set out on a course that would lead to a growing global company. On Friday, February 9, 1849, the partners officially founded the firm of Heintze & Freudenberg with an entry in the commercial registry. The revolution was put down just a few months later. Then things began to move fast. The plan worked out. Over the next three years, revenues quadrupled, and the staff grew from 50 to 170. “Three aspects play an important role here,“ Schneider says. The first is quality. “In Germany alone, there were about 10,000 companies making leather products. Freudenberg knows that he and Heintze are setting themselves apart with quality products.” Secondly, it was clear to him that he had to internationalize the business quickly to buy skins and sell leather. It was either “go big or go down,” as the saying goes. The two businessmen built up relationships in the United States, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, France and Turkey (still the Ottoman Empire at the time.) And finally, Freudenberg recognized the importance of innovation early on, picking up on the patent-leather trend from France and gearing his production operations to it. To make the change, he had to win his partner Heintze over. “If you make patent leather, you get to ride in the carriage. If you make regular leather, you walk,” he once said. He had demonstrated his farsightedness once again. The product from Weinheim was a prizewinner at the Great Exhibition in London in 1851 and secured the company’s success for years. What remains of the spirit of those early years? Or the traits of Carl Johann Freudenberg? After he bought out the Heintze family and the company became a sole proprietorship in 1874 – once again with financial help from his wife’s family – he was able to show his caring side as an entrepreneur. Heintze had been solely interested in cost-efficiency and had presumably stood in the way of his partner’s other interests. That same year, Freudenberg founded a health insurance association for his employees, the forerunner to the health insurance fund that the company later established. A general aid fund followed – it was for employees and their families who were in need. “You can see a connection to his experience as a child,” Schneider says. Friedrich Carl Freudenberg Hermann Ernst Freudenberg Freudenberg brought his sons Friedrich Carl and Hermann Ernst into the company for support, making it a family operation. In 1887, he made them partners, giving each one-third of the company. At this point, the company had more than 500 employees and substantial obligations for their care. As part of the transition to the next generation and with the size of the company in mind, Carl Johann wrote down his business principles by hand. He considered humility, honesty, a solid financial foundation, and the ability to adapt to change to be the most important principles for a successful business. The theme of trust – not just in oneself but in one’s family, partners, and employees – played a major role. To put it in Carl Johann's own words: “It is better to trust hundred times at risk of being taken in than to mistrust unjustly even once.” A summary: After misfortunes, Carl Johann Freudenberg always tried “to make the best of any situation,” (as he wrote in his Business Principles) with diligence, thrift, ambition, self-confidence, and adherence to principles. An entrepreneurial vision, the openness to change and the innovation associated with it, and a culture of trust that he personally embraced – these traits made him a successful entrepreneur whose legacy survives in the company culture down to the present. The principles that he formulated at that time are the basis of the Freudenberg Group’s Business Principles, which are applied worldwide. Freudenberg has been in family ownership for seven generations. And there are entire dynasties of employees, who have worked for the technology company for decades. Carl Johann Freudenberg, around 1862 Amidst the turmoil of the Baden Revolution, the tannery Heintze & Freudenberg is established by partners Carl Johann Freudenberg (1819-1898) and Heinrich Christian Heintze (1800-1862) on February 9, 1849. The company employs 50 workers and produces fine calf leather. A lively international trade (including exports to the USA, Great Britain, France, and Turkey) flourishes from the beginning. The ”panel field“ next to the lacquering shop in Weinheim, 1850 One year after the company is founded, Freudenberg develops its first innovation: the company begins to thrive after introducing patent leather in 1850 and develops into the largest tannery in Germany in the following years. The coat of arms of the Carl Freudenberg tannery Carl Johann Freudenberg becomes sole proprietor. The company is renamed Carl Freudenberg. In 1887 Carl Johann Freudenberg introduces the next generation. His sons, Friedrich Carl (1848–1942) and Hermann Ernst Freudenberg (1856–1923) become partners. At this time, Carl Johann Freudenberg writes down his business principles. Modesty, honesty, a solid financial foundation and the ability to adapt to the respective changes were his most important principles for successful entrepreneurship. Today, these Guiding Principles form the basis of Freudenberg’s Business Principles. Chrome tannery, 1904 Between 1900 and 1904, using his own experiments, Hermann Ernst Freudenberg develops the chrome tanning process, which is already being practiced in the US. Freudenberg is one of the first leather producers in Europe to produce high-quality, chrome-tanned calf leather. With the introduction of chrome tanning, Freudenberg becomes the largest leather manufacturer in Europe. During World War I, women took the place of their husbands, doing the latters’ work in the tannery. At the outbreak of the First World War, the company employs more than 2,500 people. Due to the sharp, war-related decline in orders and conscription for military service, the number of employees drops significantly. The women take on some of the conscripted men’s work until they return. After the war, global trade relations are re-established and expanded, even reaching South America, Asia, and Australia. First seals produced on a spindle press, 1929 The global economic crisis affects the entire leather industry in Germany, seriously threatening its viability. To secure the jobs of its more than 3,500 employees at the time, the management develops its own short-time working model. The difficult economic situation leads the management team to introduce diversification to the company with entirely new products. The first step is the introduction of leather sleeve seals for the growing auto industry in 1929. Simmerring production, 1966 Simmerring® with garter spring, 1932 With the revolutionary Simmerring®, a new era at Freudenberg begins: sealing technology. Its name is taken from the Freudenberg developer Walther Simmer. The Simmerring®, a radial shaft sealing ring for rotating shafts, replaces the felt seals previously used. Advertisement by Conrad Tack, 1939 Freudenberg takes over the shoe production and commercial chain of the Jewish-owned company Conrad Tack in Burg, near Magdeburg. Between 1933 and 1936, Freudenberg assumes control of the Gustav Hoffmann children’s shoe factory in Kleve, Germany, and its elefanten® brand. Freudenberg further expands its shoe and leather activities between 1937 and 1938 via different “Aryanizations” of Jewish companies. This also includes the equine leather business of the Jewish company Sigmund Hirsch in Weinheim, with which Freudenberg has good relations. At the time, the members of the company’s management board are civic-economic proponents of the Weimar Republic. Their outspoken criticisms of Hitler, made especially by Richard and Walter Freudenberg in 1932 and 1933, show them to have been committed democrats. However, in the years after the Nazis seize power they increasingly come to terms with the totalitarian system, to the extent that the company continues to benefit from Nazi economic policy up to the final collapse of the regime. Experiments in main laboratory, 1934 The National Socialists’ self-sufficiency efforts make it increasingly difficult to import enough rawhide for leather production. In 1934, there is therefore a leather shortage in Germany. Freudenberg responds by establishing the main laboratory. The first projects involve the utilization of skin and leather waste from the tannery and the search for leather substitutes. Research soon focuses on elastomers for the modification and further development of Buna synthetic rubber. The result is Perbunan, a base material for new Freudenberg products. Simmerring® with NBR sealing lip, 1938 Freudenberg replaces leather with rubber as a sealing material. In 1936, a sealing ring made of Perbunan/NBR is developed: It has a high temperature and swelling resistance when exposed to engine lubricating oil. The NBR Simmerring® is a quantum leap for sealing technology. Nowovens production, 1988 Nonwoven production, 1938 As a further response to the leather shortage in Germany from 1934 onwards, Freudenberg develops the synthetic latex artificial leather Viledon as a substitute material for bags and suitcases. The backing material for the artificial leather is a nonwoven that Freudenberg began developing in 1936. The synthetic rubber NBR is also used for nora® shoe soles, which are mass produced from 1938. Newspaper advertisement "The Simmerring for every application", 1942 The diversification begun before the war makes it easier to compensate for the difficult raw materials situation than in World War I, as the company is no longer exclusively in the leather business. During the war, Freudenberg is also a supplier to the armaments industry. The main products involved are gaskets for various military applications, in particular for vehicles, as well as shoes and artificial leather products for the Wehrmacht. Due to scarcity during the war, the Nazi authorities look for ways to improve the properties of shoe components. In May 1940, the Reich Office for Economic Development therefore establishes a shoe-testing track in the Sachsenhausen concentration camp. This continues to be operated by the SS as a punishment detail until the spring of 1945. Materials from at least 79 companies are tested there, one of which is Freudenberg. Because of wartime labor shortages, Freudenberg employs forced laborers between 1940 and 1945. Vileda TV commercial, 1950 At the end of the war, nonwoven backing material is refined. In 1948, production begins for nonwoven-interlinings for the textile industry and Vileda cloths made from nonwovens. At this time, the company employs more than 5,000 employees. Nonwoven production in the United States, 1953 Calendering plant for the production of floor coverings, 1964 The company expands at home and abroad. The first foreign production company is built in the USA in 1950. Interlining for the clothing industry is manufactured in Lowell, Massachusetts. This is followed by subsidiaries and investment in Great Britain, France, the rest of Europe and finally in the Far East. The company opens another product area: In 1950, the nora® rubber floor covering brand is introduced as a development of nora® shoe soles. In 2007, Freudenberg separates from its floor covering business. Production of vibration control ultra bushings, 1957 Freudenberg becomes involved in vibration control technology, which complements its expertise from sealing technology. The company produces shock absorbers, antivibration mountings and ultra bushings. In the same year, the product area of technical nonwovens is established with its first filters. Conclusion of the contract between Freudenberg and NOK, 1960 This year marks the beginning of two formative partnerships in Japan. Freudenberg forms a close partnership in sealing technology with the Nippon Oil Seal Industry Company (NOK) in Tokyo. In the nonwovens sector, Freudenberg establishes a Joint Venture with Japanese partners: the Japan Vilene Company in Tokyo. At this point, Freudenberg has more than 11,000 employees. Klüber BARRIERTA high-performance lubricant, around 1966 Freudenberg acquires Klüber Lubrication in Munich, Germany, thus opening a completely new business area with chemical products. Spunbonded nonwovens protect the crop, around 1970 The new production technology for spunbonded nonwovens, developed by the company, allows the production of nonwovens for new application areas, such as wound dressings in medical technology and nonwovens in agriculture. First micronAir® brand car cabin air filters, 1992 The first micronAir® brand car cabin air filters are introduced in 1989. Today, Freudenberg is the world market leader in car cabin air filters. The American sealing activities by Freudenberg and its Japanese partner NOK are introduced in a joint venture: the Freudenberg-NOK General Partnership (FNGP). Sensor Simmerring with integrated encoder, 1997 The Simmerring® takes on additional functions. Encoder technology is developed and the seal becomes a product that performs tasks beyond sealing. With integrated sensor technology, the encoder can measure the engine revolutions, making it possible to control anti-lock braking systems (ABS) and engine management systems. In the same year, Freudenberg Politex Nonwovens SpA is established in Novedrate, Italy to produce polyester nonwovens made from recycled PET bottles. In 2004, Freudenberg assumes 100% control of the joint venture with Italian partners. Components for fuel cells: gas diffusion layers and seals, 2009 Freudenberg Fuel Cell Components Technology is established in 2001. This new business combines the competencies that have been built up in various Freudenberg activities since the 1990s. It develops components – including seals, gas diffusion layers, filters and humidifiers – for fuel cells, a promising energy technology. At this time, the company employs around 30,000 people. Leather production in Weinheim, 1997 Freudenberg bids farewell to its original leather business. Business relocations, reductions in production by large customers and a sharp rise in commodity prices have made the business unprofitable. Burgmann mechanical seal, 2004 With the acquisition of Burgmann Dichtungswerke based in Wolfratshausen near Munich, Germany, Freudenberg expands its sealing business to become a specialist in mechanical seals. Il Decreto prevede l’esclusione di responsabilità delle Società solo qualora dimostri che: il Consiglio di Amministrazione / Organo Dirigente ha adottato ed efficacemente attuato, prima della commissione del fatto, un Modello idoneo a prevenire reati della specie di quello verificatosi; il compito di vigilare sul funzionamento e l’osservanza del Modello e di curare il loro aggiornamento è stato affidato ad un organismo dell’ente dotato di autonomi poteri di iniziativa e di controllo (Organismo di Vigilanza); le persone hanno commesso il reato eludendo fraudolentemente il Modello; non vi è stata omessa o insufficiente vigilanza da parte dell’Organismo di Vigilanza. Nell’ambito delle proprie attività, Freudenberg ha identificato alcuni valori di riferimento, principi generali cui devono attenersi i dipendenti e coloro che operano per conto delle Società al fine di assicurare la correttezza nella conduzione degli affari, nelle attività sociali, per tutelare il patrimonio e la reputazione aziendale e rispettare l’ambiente circostante. Tutti i Modelli sono suddivisi in una Parte Generale, contenente le prescrizioni del Decreto Legislativo, e in una Parte Speciale nella quale sono riportate le finalità del Modello, l’individuazione delle attività a rischio, le regole comportamentali di carattere generale che devono essere osservate al fine di prevenire il rischio di commissione dei reati associati alle attività aziendali, le caratteristiche e il funzionamento dell’Organismo di Vigilanza, i flussi informativi, l’attività di formazione e informazione, il sistema disciplinare. Compressed air is used to clean the products of fibers or particles. Digital Monitoring Extends Seal Lifespan Seals play a crucial yet often unnoticed role. In applications like transcontinental pipelines, they can be difficult to access or located far from service teams. Freudenberg Flow Technologies' digital monitoring systems provide continuous oversight of sealing systems, allowing parameters such as pressure, temperature, and vibrations to be monitored remotely. Battery-powered sensors are attached directly to the seal's inlets and outlets or even placed inside the seal itself. The collected data is transmitted wirelessly, monitored, and analyzed. If any values exceed predefined limits, an alarm is triggered, and the customer is notified. This proactive monitoring helps prevent subsequent damage, costly repairs, and excessive material and resource use. ETHICS OFFICEs Freudenberg Group Whistleblower Solution and Complaints Procedure The Ethics Offices are a confidential contact center for all Freudenberg employees and third parties (i.e. individuals outside the Freudenberg Group, such as suppliers or customers) who would like to report an actual or imminent violation of laws or the Corporate Principles applicable at Freudenberg (Business and Guiding Principles, our Code of Conduct and supplementary internal regulations). Contact the Ethics Offices confidentially: Reporting system Extern url The purpose of the Ethics Offices is to ensure that the Freudenberg Group conducts its business in compliance with the laws and its principles, thereby protecting the Freudenberg Group from liability risks and reputational damage and its managers and employees from personal liability. Detection and correction of misconduct help the Freudenberg Group in implementing essential principles of good corporate governance and support the Freudenberg Group in fulfilling its corporate human rights responsibility along global supply chains at the same time. The Ethics Offices are accessible to everyone: Members of a Freudenberg Group company, as well as third parties, may report any committed or imminent company-related violation of laws or breaches of our Corporate Principles, or any other internal or external guidelines and local practices. Such violations include bribery and corruption or non-compliance with anti-trust, environmental protection, safety or labor laws. Information providers may also report human rights and environment-related risks and violations pursuant to the German Act on Corporate Due Diligence Obligations in Supply Chains (so called Complaints Procedure) that have arisen as a result of the economic actions of Freudenberg in its own business area or the actions of a direct or indirect supplier of Freudenberg. The Freudenberg Group has one central Ethics Office in Europe ( Corporate Ethics Office ) and three regional Ethics Offices ( Regional Ethics Offices Asia, India and Americas ). You may reach the Ethics Offices via the electronic reporting system. Every day, more than 45,000 people work together to ensure that Freudenberg’s success story remains one of innovation. The idea of excellence and entrepreneurial vision has been part of the Group’s DNA ever since Carl Johann Freudenberg founded the company in 1849. Freudenberg is successful through change. The company is evolving daily. Founded as a tannery, the Group’s first diversification was driven by the Simmerring. Today, Freudenberg is well established in more than 30 markets and thousands of applications. International history of Freudenberg Freudenberg in Brazil Business relations with Brazil date back almost to the beginnings of the Freudenberg Group itself. 1853-54 Business relationship with Ziese & Co. in Rio de Janeiro (purchase of skins and leather sales) 1912 there has been a general agent for Latin and South America (purchasing and sales) including Brazil with P. Oberstgab Entry into the Brazilian market didn’t take place until 1958 1958: In Agudos / Brazil an abandoned coffee plantation is acquired and afforested. Following that a wood-working factory (chipboard, veneer) is built in its place. 1958-1972 Agreements with the Orion company in São Paulo, Brazil, for the manufacture of seals. 1971 Klüber Lubrication Indústria e Comércio Ltda. in Barneri, S.P. founded. 1973-1985 Gustav Hoffmann takes a stake in the Brazilian childrens’ shoe factory Calcados Ortopé S.A. in Gramado/Brazil. 1973 Stake in the sealing factory Rubrasil S.A. in São Paulo established in 1958. 1973 Stake Recouro S.A , Rio de Janeiro, (reclaimed leather products). The stake was sold in 1984. 1985 Acquisition of Intece in Jacareí, Brazil from the French company Chargeurs (today Freudenberg Não Tecidos Ltda.). 1985-1987 Reorganisation of corporate legal structure for CAFMA, FIMSA and Intece (Partnerships). 1988 With the involvement of Freudenberg and NOK, Rubrasil was renamed Freudenberg NOK – Componentes Ltda. The Brazilian wood operations were sold. 1998 The Joint Venture Vibracoustic do Brasil Ltda. was founded with Woco do Brasil Ltda. 2013 Freudenberg Filtration Technologies opens a new production facility in Jacarei, Brazil. The Freudenberg Regional Corporate Center South America, headquartered in Alphaville near São Paulo is opened. Like many things at Freudenberg, the company’s links to Asia have a long tradition. Initially this was due to the special product manufactured in Weinheim: leather. In the 19th century, Carl Freudenberg already had business partners in China (Hong Kong) who marketed the leather which had received awards at a number of World’s Fairs. 1923 Freudenberg products (leather) are represented in China by Melchers. 1977 Freudenberg & Vilene International Ltd. Hong Kong, is established in Hong Kong. The company Freudenberg Trading Hong Kong Ltd. is established for sales. 1980 Klüber Lubrication China Ltd. is established in Hong Kong. 1987 In Taiwan, Freudenberg Lutravil Far East, later known as Far Eastern Spunweb, is established with Japanese and Chinese partners. The company starts production in 1990. 1989 Taiwan Vilene Company (later known as Freudenberg & Vilene Nonwovens (Taiwan) Co. Ltd.) is established with Japan Vilene Company and partners in Taiwan. 1994 In China, the development of Changchun NOK-Freudenberg Oilseal Co., Ltd. in Changchun starts in 1994; Wuxi NOK-Freudenberg Oilseal Co. Ltd. is established in Wuxi. The plant is inaugurated in September 1996. 1995 In Suzhou (People’s Republic of China), Freudenberg and Japan Vilene Company together found Freudenberg & Vilene Nonwovens as a production facility for interlinings. The plant is inaugurated in August 1996. 1996 Foundation of Freudenberg & Vilene International (Shanghai) Trading Co., Ltd. NOK-Freudenberg Hong Kong Ltd. is founded in Kowloon for the sale of sealing products. 1998 Foundation of Freudenberg Household Products (Suzhou) Co., Ltd. 2002 Foundation of Klüber Lubrication (Shanghai) Co. Ltd. 2005 Freudenberg Dichtungs- und Schwingungstechnik KG establishes NOK-Freudenberg Group Sales (China) Co., Ltd and NOK-Freudenberg Group Trading (China) Co., Ltd as sales companies together with NOK. NOK-Freudenberg Co. Ltd is founded for fluid seals. 2008 In Qingpu, China (near Shanghai), Klüber Lubrication and ChemTrend construct a new factory for the production of lubricants and release agents. Freudenberg NOK GP acquires Anura Plastics Engineering in Baldwin Park/CA with facilities in the USA und China (Shenzen/Guandong) to expand the medical products sector. 2011 Freudenberg Household Products continues to expand in Asia. The business of Trade & Investment in Asia Limited (TIA) with facilities in China, Hong Kong, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia and Taiwan is acquired in 2011. Merkel NOK Freudenberg inaugurates a new production plant for polyurethane seals in Taicang/China, near Shanghai. Polyurethane seals are used in industrial applications and automotive hydraulic systems. Freudenberg Filtration Technologies starts to construct a new plant in Chengdu/China (Sichuan Province) together with Japan Vilene Group (JVC). Freudenberg Vilene Filter produces engine air intake and cabin air filters there from August 2012. Freudenberg Filtration Technologies inaugurates its first laboratory for the development of automobile interior filters in China at its facility in Suzhou. 2012 At the beginning of December, NOK-Freudenberg Group China inaugurates a plant in Wuxi. The plant mainly produces Simmerrings and O-rings as well as Bellows and flat seals. 2014 The Qingpu site expansion with state-of-the-art research and development facilities, a training center and administration building for Freudenberg Chemical Specialities. 1920 Freudenberg starts business relations with India – for raw material purchasing. 1950 Hide imports from India start again. 1954 The first Simrit branch for India opens in Bombay (today known as Mumbai). 1973 Establishment of Burgmann Industries India (today EgaleBurgmann). 1989 OKS production site in Mysore opens. Merger with Klüber India takes place later. 1995 NOK and Freudenberg establish NOK-Fredenberg Asia Holding C. Pte. Ltd. in Singapore to administer activities in India and China. 1998 Nonwovens KG establishes a distribution company in India. It’s called Freudenberg Nonwovens India Private Ltd. and is based in Mumbai (Bombay). 1999 Klüber founds Klüber Lubrication India Pvt. Ltd in Mumbai. 2000 Freudenberg Sealing and Vibration Control Technology forms a joint venture with SIGMA and NOK in Mohali / India (Sigma Freudenberg NOK PVT. Ltd.). 2003 The first seal production plant opens in Mohali, India. In the years to come, India becomes one of the key growth markets for Freudenberg. 2006 SurTec Chemicals India is established in Pune. 2008 KE-Burgmann Flexibles India opens a new production site for compensators in Chhahattisgarth/India. Freudenberg Household Products establishes a joint venture in India with its Indian partner Gala Brush Limited – Freudenberg Gala Household Products Pvt. Limited with headquarters in Mumbai. Freudenberg Filtration Technologies concludes a partnership agreement with its Indian partner Thermax for the manufacture of combined filter and cooling solutions for large gas-driven turbines and compressors. Vibracoustic starts production of air springs at its site in Mohali / India. Klüber Lubrication starts with the expansion of production at its site in Mysore. 2012 Freudenberg Filtration Technologies India in Pune acquires Pyramid Filters – a special filter manufacturer. 2013 EagleBurgmann India opens a new, fully-automated and computer-managed test plant in Pune. Opening of the Freudenberg Regional Corporate Center India in Bangalore. 1849 When the new firm of Heintze & Freudenberg is founded, a flourishing trade with the USA starts. 1853 Bronze Medal for good leather at the EXHIBITION OF THE INDUSTRY OF ALL NATIONS in New York. 1874-1876 Hermann Ernst Freudenberg, third son and later Managing Director of Carl Freudenberg, spends his apprentice years in Milwaukee, Chicago and Boston. 1903-1904 Walter Freudenberg, second son of the Managing Director Friedrich Carl Freudenberg, rounds off his training as a raw materials purchaser in America. 1914 Hermann Ernst Freudenberg, together with his son Otto, visits the USA in order to acquire new accounts. 1926 Acquisition of the Western Hide & Skin Corporation in Los Angeles as a purchasing company for tannery raw materials. The company was relocated to Panama in 1950, and liquidated in 1972. 1929 First foundation of an American sales company: Carl Freudenberg Inc. Boston. The firm was liquidated in 1935 under the laws of the Third Reich, and its capital transferred to the Reichsbank. 1950-1951 First company founded abroad after the war with an American partner: Pellon Corporation in Lowell, Mass., for producing interlinings. It was the first production site outside of Germany. 1955 Cooperation with Greer Hydraulics for producing polyurethane components. The firm is subsequently transferred to Freudenberg’s sole ownership, and from 1957 onwards produces polyurethane precision moldings and hydraulic components under the name of Disogrin. It is integrated into FNGP in 1989. 1960 Agreement with the Leather's Best company for selling Freudenberg leather. In 1965, acquisition of a 45 % holding, which in 1981 is sold back to the partner Chilewich. 1961 Acquisition of the tannery Teneria TEMOLA in Cuautla, Mexico. In 1981, the majority was sold to a partner, followed in 1992 by the remaining shares as well. 1967 Foundation of the subsidiary elBe Products for selling nonwovens and synthetics. 1968 First holding purchased in International Packings Corp. in Bristol, NH. Subsequently, Freudenberg acquired all the stock, and incorporated the firm into FNGP in 1989. 1972 Foundation of Pellon Chemotextiles in Cornwall, Canada, with an American partner (sold in 1987.) 1975 Foundation of SIMRIT DE MEXICO with the partner Irurita. 1978 Foundation of the sales company Simrit Corporation in Arlington Heights, which is integrated into FNGP in 1989. 1979 Acquisition of Escan Corp. in Escanaba for producing vibration control components. It is integrated into FNGP in 1989. 1981 Foundation of Lutravil Company for producing spunbonded nonwovens, in Durham NC, with an American partner. From 1986 onwards wholly owned by Freudenberg, today operating as Freudenberg Spunweb Company. 1989 Foundation of FNGP with NOK as partner, grouping together all the seals and vibration control technology firms. 1990 In Port Washington/USA, elefanten GmbH sets up a joint venture with Allen Edmonds for producing children’s footwear. 1991 Acquisition of Woodland Molded Plastics Corp. in Broadview/Ill. In 1994, the firm is incorporated into the new Auttocom L.L.C., Wilmington. Auttocom L.L.C. is merged with FNGP in 1996. The premises are sold. 1996 Klüber Lubrication Munich acquires the lubricant company Sum-mit Industrial Products in Tyler/Texas. 1998 Freudenberg Haushaltsprodukte KG takes over from M.B. Walton in River Grove/Ill. a production operation for floor-cleaning equipment, with a workforce of 120. The new subsidiary is called Freudenberg Household Products LP. The Freudenberg Nonwovens Group signs a cooperation agreement with the North American company Milliken in Spartanburg covering the NAFTA region, for producing woven and knitted fabrics. Freudenberg NOK GP acquires the O-ring specialist International Seal Corporation with plants in Los Angeles and Henderson/Nevada, and sales companies in Mexico, Australia and Canada. 2003 Freudenberg IT KG founds the US subsidiary Freudenberg IT LP. Besides the facility in Plymouth near Detroit (Michigan), a computer center is also opened in Durham (North Carolina). As it expands on the international stage, the IT service provider does increasing business with globally operating clients. Freudenberg Haushaltsprodukte KG purchases the American firm O-Cedar Brands, so as to gain further ground in America. It is integrated into Freudenberg Household Products LP in Northlake/Illinois. 2004 Klüber Lubrication purchases from Foseco GmbH the American subsidiary Chem Trend in Howell, Michigan, founded in 1960, which produces parting agents. In Manchester/New Hampshire, Freudenberg forms a Corporate Center for North America. 2006 FNGP acquires the Imperial Rubber and Urethane Corporation in Nisku/Canada for the production of technical solutions for the oil and gas industry. Helix Medical LLC in Carpinteria/California, a manufacturer of high-quality and precision molded parts as well as tubes for the medical technology, pharma and biotech markets, was also acquired by FNGP. 2008 FNGP acquires Anura Plastics Engineering in Balwin Park/CA with sites in USA and China (Shenzen/Guandong) to strengthen the health care business. Freudenberg Nonwovens closes the nonwoven production in Hopkinsville, Kentucky/USA and transferred it to Durham, North Carolina/USA. Simrit Division USA acquires the Tetralene company, a developer and producer of customer-specific sealing components for the oil and gas industry. FNGP closes the site Laconia in New Hampshire, USA. 2011 Foundation of Freudenberg Sealing Technologies (FST). Under the roof of FST the activities of Freudenberg Dichtungs- und Schwingungstechnik Europa and der Freudenberg-NOK General Partnership are united. FNGP is renamed in Freudenberg-NOK Sealing Technologies (FNST). Freudenberg Household Products founded the joint venture company FHP-Berner with the SP Berner Plastic Group S.L., Valencia/Spain. FHP-Berner opens a production site in Aurora/USA close to Chicago. 2012 Freudenberg IT opens a new data processing center in North Carolina, USA. Helix Medical acquires the American MedVenture Technology Corporation seated in Jeffersonville, Indiana, USA. Across the globe, the Freudenberg Group’s products and services make a valuable contribution to the success of its customers – rarely visible, but always indispensable. Freudenberg is a diversified technology company with a very broad product spectrum, ranging from seals and nonwovens to household products, lubricants and IT services. Freudenberg mainly supplies intermediate products for further processing or to be used in manufacturing final goods. Although mostly hidden from view, our products are always indispensable.​ Our household products, including brands such as Vileda and, O-Cedar, are marketed directly to consumers. Freudenberg produces seals and vibration control components for many different industry sectors, of which the automotive industry is the company’s largest customer. Verantwortung für die Gesellschaft Seiteninhalt ​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​Für uns bedeutet Erfolg mehr als nur Erfolg am Markt: Wirklich erfolgreich sind wir, wenn wir unsere wirtschaftlichen Ziele erreichen und gleichzeitig Verantwortung gegenüber der Gesellschaft übernehmen. Diese beiden Ziele sind untrennbar miteinander verknüpft und seit mehr als 165 Jahren in unseren Unternehmenswerten verankert.​ ​ Compliance, Menschenrechte & Arbeitsnormen, Nachhaltigkeit, Arbeits- und Gesundheitsschutz, Umweltschutz sowie gesellschaftliches Engagement sind in unseren Werten und Grundsätzen verankert, insbesondere im Wert „Verantwortung“. Diese fünf Bereiche sind eng miteinander verknüpft und drücken sich in unserer Verantwortung für die Gesellschaft aus.​

Im Rahmen eines Sustainability-Projekts haben wir für Freudenberg eine gruppenweite Definition entwickelt: Wir wollen unseren Footprint verkleinern und unseren Handprint für unsere Kunden und die Endverbraucher vergrößern. Das bedeutet, dass wir die negativen Folgen unserer Produktionsprozesse für die Umwelt minimieren (Footprint) und die Nachhaltigkeit unserer Kunden durch unsere nachhaltigen Produkte und Services fördern (Handprint). Dabei setzen wir sowohl beim Footprint als auch beim Handprint auf Ressourceneffizienz.​ Zum einen geht es darum, wie das Unternehmen selbst seine Prozesse anpasst, Rohstoffe beschafft und einsetzt, Anlagen ausrüstet und Verfahrenstechniken neuen Bedürfnissen anpasst, um möglichst ressourcenschonend zu produzieren. Hier sprechen wir davon, unseren Footprint zu minimieren. Zum anderen bietet Freudenberg zahlreiche Produkte und Lösungen an, die es Kunden erlauben, effizienter und nachhaltiger zu fertigen, die Umweltbilanz ihrer Produkte zu verbessern oder eigene Nachhaltigkeitsziele zu realisieren. Hier bewirkt Freudenberg einen positven Handprint.​ Nachhaltigkeit ​ ist für Freudenberg nichts Neues, sondern seit jeher Teil unserer Unternehmenswerte. Unsere Werte und Grundsätze sind die Basis für die Verantwortung der Freudenberg Gruppe gegenüber der Gesellschaft. Nachhaltigkeit als ein Teil dessen, gibt uns die Möglichkeit, diesen Anspruch zu erfüllen – und das bereits seit mehr als 165 Jahren.​ Gemeinsam mit unseren Kunden, Partnern und der Wissenschaft entwickeln wir technisch führende Produkte, Lösungen und Services und leisten einen Beitrag, die Lebensbedingungen der Menschen weltweit zu verbessern. Unser fortwährendes Streben nach mehr Nachhaltigkeit stärkt unsere Innovationskraft​. Zugleich machen Innovationen nachhaltigere Prozesse und Produkte erst möglich. Innovation und bedingen sich also und treiben einander voran. Innovationen können einen Beitrag zu Nachhaltigkeit leisten, indem sie sich unmittelbar positiv auf unseren Footprint und Handprint auswirken. Grundsätzlich gilt: Je innovativer wir sind, desto nachhaltiger können unsere eigenen Prozesse sowie unsere Produkte werden. Je nachhaltiger unsere Produkte, desto größer der Handprint für unsere Kunden und für die Endverbraucher der Freudenberg-Produkte. Die Geschäftsgruppen der Unternehmensgruppe setzen die oben genannten Leitsätze als Grundlage ihres unternehmerischen Handelns um. Informationen hierzu finden Sie u.a. auf der Website der jeweiligen Geschäftsgruppe . Ansprechpartner für die gesamte Freudenberg Gruppe und insbesondere für den Arbeits-, Gesundheits- und Umweltschutz ist die Konzernfunktion Corporate Health, Safety and Environmental Protection. Freudenberg veröffentlicht einen jährlichen Geschäftsbericht zur Bilanz des Unternehmens einschließlich einer Rubrik zu „Verantwortung“ bei Freudenberg. Freudenberg veröffentlicht als Mitglied der Global Compact-Initiative der Vereinten Nationen einen Fortschrittsbericht Freundeberg verfügt außerdem über ein umfangreiches internes Berichtswesen unter anderem für die Themenfelder Gesundheits-, Arbeits- und Umweltschutz; Auszüge daraus werden auf dieser Webseite, im Geschäftsbericht der Unternehmensgruppe und im Fortschrittsbericht veröffentlicht. Verantwortlich für Arbeitsschutz sind alle Mitarbeiter und alle Führungskräfte in allen Ebenen und Bereichen. Sie werden dabei durch die HSE-Organisationen der Geschäftsgruppen und deren Standorte, sowie durch die Konzernfunktion Corporate Health, Safety, Security, Environment unterstützt. Mehr als 80% der Produktionsstandorte von Freudenberg verfügen über ein Arbeitsschutz-Managementsystem (OHSAS 18001). Neben Themen wie „Sicherheit von Maschinen“, „sichere Materialien“ „persönlicher Schutz-Ausrüstung für Mitarbeitern und Sicherheit für Kontraktoren steht bei Freudenberg die Förderung einer Sicherheitskultur sowie das sichere Verhalten aller Mitarbeiter im Fokus. Mehr als 80% der Produktionsstandorte von Freudenberg verfügen über ein Umwelt-managementsystem (ISO 14001 oder EMAS*). Daneben setzen wir bei Freudenberg diverse Audits, Kennzahlen usw. gruppenweit ein, um die Umwelt-Auswirkungen der Unternehmensgruppe kontinuierlich zu verringern. Freudenberg will dazu beitragen, das Klima zu schützen, und seine erzeugten Schadstoffemissionen, wo immer technisch und wirtschaftlich möglich und insbesondere seine spezifischen Kohlendioxid-(CO2-)Emissionen kontinuierlich senken. Die Unterstützungserklärung, die jeweils der Vorstandsvorsitzende des Unternehmens unterzeichnet, ist an den UN-Generalsekretär Ban Ki-moon gerichtet. „Freudenberg handelt seit jeher werteorientiert und nachhaltig. As part of the Sustainability Project, we have developed a Group-wide definition for Freudenberg: We strive to minimize our Footprint and maximize the Handprint for our customers and end-users. That means we are minimizing the environmental impact from the company's manufacturing processes (Footprint) and maximizing our impact as a Sustainability enabler at our customers (Handprint) by providing sustainable products and services. Find out more about our understanding of Sustainability and read about current examples​ from the Freudenberg world. ​The first is how the company itself adapts its processes, obtains and allocates resources, equips its plants and aligns its process technologies with new needs to make production as resource-friendly as possible. We call this minimizing the Footprint. The second dimension relates to the numerous products and services Freudenberg delivers to customers to enable them to improve efficiency and Sustainability or the eco-balance of their own products and to achieve their own Sustainability goals. This is where Freudenberg contributes to a positive Handprint.​ Sustainability is nothing new to Freudenberg but has been part of our corporate values for years. Our Values and Principles have always embraced the Group's responsibility for society. Sustainability is one way in which we demonstrate this responsibility – and have been doing so for over 165 years. Together with our customers, our partners and the world of science, we develop leading-edge products, solutions and services and contribute to improving the living conditions of people worldwide. The constant quest for increased Sustainability is a key driver for Innovation. At the same time, Innovation results in more sustainable processes and products. The one drives the other. Innovation can contribute to Sustainability by having a direct positive impact on our Footprint and Handprint. Fundamentally, the more we innovate, the more sustainable our processes and products become. The more sustainable our products, the larger the Handprint will be for our customers and the end-users of Freudenberg products.​ The Business Groups of the Freudenberg Group take the Guiding Principles mentioned above as the foundation for their business activities. You can find further details on the websites of the various Business Groups. The contact point for the entire Freudenberg Group, especially with regard to Health, Safety and Environmental Protection, is the Corporate HSE Function.​​ Freudenberg publishes an Annual Report that not only includes the financial statements of the Group but also a section on "Responsibility". As a member of the United Nations Global Compact​ initiative, Freudenberg publishes a progress report . Freudenberg has a comprehensive internal reporting system that also covers the topics of health, safety and environmental protection. Excerpts from these internal reports are published on this website, in the Group's annual report and the progress report. All employees on all levels and in all units are responsible for safety at work. They are supported in their efforts by the HSE organisations of the locations and Business Groups, as well as the Corporate Functions of the parent company Freudenberg & Co. More than 80 % of Freudenberg’s production locations have a safety at work management system (OHSAS 18001). In addition to topics such as machine safety, safe materials, personal protective equipment for employees and safety for contractors, Freudenberg focuses on a safety culture and safe behaviour by all employees. More than 80 percent of Freudenberg's production locations have an environmental management system (ISO 14001 or EMAS*). In addition, Freudenberg uses a variety of audits and performance indicators to continually reduce the environmental impact of the Group's activities. Freudenberg wants to systematically reduce the harmful emissions it generates, especially CO2 emissions, wherever this is technically and commercially possible, making a contribution to the protection of the environment. You can find more information about this topic in the HSE Guidline. *Eco-Management and Audit Scheme On the basis of our HSE organisation, we ensure a responsible approach to health protection at all our facilities. Depending on the type and size of the plant, measures range from the provision of first aid assistance and organisations to company ambulances. In line with its approach to safety, Freudenberg focuses on prevention in the field of occupational health. In addition, therapeutic and rehabilitation measures are taken when appropriate. Crisis management is incorporated into the Business Group’s and operational units’ crisis and risk management systems. Included is the necessity to raise awareness for fire prevention and to avoid operational disruption and supply shortages. In our Guiding Principles , we explain the principle of "Value for customers" and present our general position on our relationship with external stakeholders. Our view of responsibility for society is also described in our Responsibility​ principle. We do not tolerate illegal or unethical conduct and take active measures to avoid it. We encourage our business partners, (sub)-contractors and suppliers to act in accordance with the responsibility principle.* We will not manufacture any products intended for harming people (e.g. weapons).** The existing International Labor Organisation (ILO) agreement forms a guideline for the Freudenberg Group. This includes, in particular, the following agreements with regard to the prevention / decrees of Equal opportunity and non-discrimination at work, in accordance with ILO conventions 100 and 111; Freedom of association, protection of the right to organize and the right to collective bargaining in accordance with ILO conventions 87 and 98. Forced labor in accordance with the ILO conventions definition, 29 and 105. Child labor and minimum age in accordance with the ILO convention definition, 138 and 182. The right of Freudenberg Group employees to join a trade union, to choose employee representation and representation of common interests in collective bargaining is recognized. ILO convention 131 forms the basis of this: Freedom of association, collective bargaining and industrial relations. *( Values & Principles ) **( Business Principles )​ We strive to exceed the requirements of applicable laws and regulations: that is, to work and behave in such a manner that compliance with the minimum standards required by applicable law is never in doubt. Strict compliance with laws is essential and does not allow any scope for discretion. The Code of Conduct, valid for all employees of the Freudenberg Group worldwide, reflects the benefit statement (“Freudenberg is a values-based technology group that best serves its customers and society”) and is based on the Group’s Guiding Principles and Business Principles. The Code of Conduct contains clear guidelines with regard to law-abiding and responsible behavior conduct. So that all employees are able to read and understand the Code of Conduct, it has been translated into 25 languages. Any benefit secured from an infringement of the Group’s Guiding Principles, or conduct that runs contrary to the Guiding Principles is not desired. The Freudenberg Group signed the United Nations Global Compact in January 2014. Responsibility Society At STIHL we are firmly convinced that companies have a special responsibility to society. We gladly accept this responsibility – not only at our founding company in Waiblingen but also at our national and international subsidiaries. By initiating and supporting social and cultural projects we make a contribution to a positive development of society. SOS-Kinderdorf e.V. (SOS Children's Villages) STIHL supports SOS-Kinderdorf e.V. Over the past few years the STIHL workforce has been engaged in a number of fund-raising campaigns in aid of SOS children's villages in crisis regions. We support this involvement and top up the amounts collected. Furthermore, STIHL is directly involved on the spot in Germany. STIHL staff help to look after the grounds in SOS children's villages. The sponsoring partnership of our subsidiary VIKING and SOS children's villages in Austria has existed since 2004. In the last few years VIKING has campaigned for different SOS children's villages in Austria as well as other countries. In addition, the company supports children's villages throughout Austria with donations in kind. Young Trainees in Rio de Janeiro‘s Botanical Garden Rio de Janeiro's botanical garden is one of the most important of its kind in the world. The 200-year-old Jardim Bontânico do Rio de Janeiro, as it is called in Portuguese, offers a habitat for several thousand species, some of which are threatened. Cooperating with the Botanical Garden Research Institute, the Rio de Janeiro State Court and the Friends of the Botanical Garden Society, STIHL Brazil supports the Pró-Florescer project. In Pró-Florescer, 70 young people from socially disadvantaged backgrounds are trained as park guides, gardeners or administrative assistants. During their training, the young adults are given free board and lodging and clothing. In addition, they receive pocket money. Apart from acquiring technical know-how, the participants develop their community spirit, initiative and self-confidence. A team of specialists, teachers and psychologists accompany the training and assist the freshly trained young men and women in finding a job. The botanical garden also profits from Pró-Florescer: It has 70 additional workers – equipped with STIHL products. STIHL Brazil has been involved as a project partner since the early nineties. STIHL sponsors ten training places every year and supports the project with numerous donations, such as cordless electric products and personal protective equipment. Together we are strong Sport brings people together – it was with this thought in mind that the Special Olympics Germany was founded in 1991. The aim is to inspire mentally and physically impaired people to take part in sports and, at the same time, give them the opportunity to participate in the life of society. The purpose is not only to win medals, but to convey the joy of living and the fun of sports and thus improve independence and the quality of life. STIHL has been supporting the Special Olympics State Association in Rhineland-Palatinate since 2006, for social inclusion is a subject very close to STIHL‘s heart. Working together with Special Olympics, we want to strengthen the acceptance of people with disabilities. At the state games, about 1,300 athletes compete in 14 events and show that sport can transcend borders and bring down barriers. Schule meets High School Overcoming language barriers and finding new friends There has been a student exchange program between the Staufer Grammar School in Waiblingen and Tallwood High School in Virginia Beach since 2012. STIHL and its US subsidiary STIHL Inc. made a significant contribution to establishing the program. This is now an annual event on the calendar. Waiblingen students get to know the life of an American high school student for two weeks. They live with an American family, attend school with their American counterparts and go on excursions in the area. A few months later the young students from Virginia Beach come to stay with the families of the German students. The participants are invited to visit the local STIHL plant in both America and Germany. STIHL and STIHL Inc. support the exchange program financially, too. It's not all that it seems The touring exhibition "Good Looks. No Substance" informs consumers about the dangers of counterfeit products for people, society and the economy. It is organized by the Aktionskreis gegen Produkt- und Markenpiraterie e.V. (Anti Product Piracy Association) (APM). In Germany alone, the damage caused annually by product and brand piracy amounts to an estimated 50 billion euros. This initially affects companies – but it ultimately results in a loss of jobs and tax revenue. However, the counterfeits present an even greater risk to consumers: It is no longer just luxury watches or handbags that are being forged, but also pharmaceuticals, foods and technical equipment, such as STIHL chainsaws. Outwardly, the illegal copies can be hardly distinguished from the originals, but are of a poorer quality and finish and, at worst, can jeopardize the health and safety of the user. The aim of this APM project is to inform consumers and create an awareness of the dangers of product and brand piracy. STIHL supports the exhibition which has been seen at more than 60 shopping centers so far. Formula 1 in Schools Tomorrow's engineers In the multidisciplinary and international "Formula 1 in Schools" technology competition teams of students design and build a miniature F1 racing car, which they then put through its paces on the racetrack. The teams compete against each other at regional contests and the German championships. Judging includes not just sheer vehicle speed, but also the design, manufacture, reaction time, business plan and a presentation. The aim is to inspire young people to take up technical and engineering careers. STIHL has been sponsoring a regional team since 2012 with donations, know-how and materials. In 2014, the team qualified for the World Finals in Singapore with an outstanding performance at the German championships.
